judgments.rationale: Complex-exponential algebra is the largest coherent block (parts (c)-(e)); the differential equation, trigonometric identities, and hyperbola/rotation graph work are separately marked supporting methods.

The system is solved through first- and higher-order linear differential equations, and the markscheme explicitly awards differentiating the system and solving the resulting equations; integration and function-inverse labels are not independently assessed.
The entire five-mark task is evaluation of a definite integral by finding an antiderivative and applying the limits; no separate limit, series, or function skill is marked.

Geometric and arithmetic sequence conditions account for the main work. The convergence/infinite-sum limit component is retained as a distinct Calculus secondary skill, with ownership kept separate from the Number-and-algebra sequence label.

Maclaurin expansions and the final limit dominate, while the definite integral approximation and explicitly differentiated auxiliary function are also marked Calculus methods. A Number-and-algebra series tag would duplicate the same series work.
After composition is written down, the substantive five-mark task solves a trigonometric equation and selects the domain-valid solutions. Composition is not an independently controlled skill here.
The product-rule derivative is explicitly marked and is then applied to a tangent-parallel condition, so both differentiation technique and its tangent application are material.

The two transformations are explicitly requested and the remaining marks use amplitude, minimum, and intercept behavior of the transformed graph. Both graph analysis and geometric transformation are assessed.
Both marks-bearing parts find the normalizing constant and expectation from a continuous probability density; integration is the computation method, not a separate assessed topic.
The median and standard deviation of a frequency table are the only requested methods, so descriptive statistics is sufficient; probability models is not independently assessed.
Volume of revolution, filling time, and the related-rate calculation account for most marks; deriving and using the inverse function is an independently marked secondary function method.

Normal probabilities are used throughout, conditional probability is explicitly requested in (c)(ii), and the exact-five binomial calculation is a discrete random-variable method. No independent Number-and-algebra counting topic is needed.

Euler approximation, substitution, separation/solution, and interpretation of the solution curve all serve the explicitly stated differential-equation problem; logarithms are an intermediate algebraic step.
The segment is found as sector area minus triangle area and the final equation is solved in radians; coordinate geometry is not independently assessed.
Rest/change-of-direction and acceleration use the velocity model and its derivative, while total distance is found by integrating with a sign change. Both marked Calculus applications are material.

The question uses independence to construct event probabilities and then explicitly asks for a conditional probability, making both probability-model reasoning and conditional probability materially assessed.

The four-mark assessed task solves a rational inequality by locating intersections and sign intervals; the two-mark odd-function observation is supporting context rather than an independently retained function skill.
All parts use vector magnitudes, parallel/opposite directions, perpendicularity, and scalar products; the quadratic equation arising in the last part is not independently assessed.
The product of roots and the sign condition reduce directly to a quadratic rational inequality in k.

The question explicitly assesses polygonal-number formulae, arithmetic-series structure, quadratic solving in the common-number search, and a long induction proof. The dot diagrams are illustrative, not triangle geometry.
Derivative/tangent and inflection-point work form the largest coherent assessed block. Polynomial/complex-root reasoning and the requested curve sketch are distinct secondary methods.
The rational-function sketch, inverse derivation/domain, and composition with arctan are function and graph/inverse tasks. No calculus or quadratic topic is independently assessed.

The Argand diagram, conjugate product, equilateral-root relation, and quadratic-root restriction are complex-number algebra; the triangle description supplies context rather than a separate geometry method.
Asymptotes, intercepts, sketching, and reading the rational-function branches are primary; the two subsequent rational inequalities are independently assessed algebraic inequality work.
The only task is solving a shifted cosine equation for the least positive radian value. Radian units are required but no sector/arc method is assessed.
The coefficient is obtained from the binomial expansion and the mean-term condition becomes a quadratic whose two valid x-values are required.

The six-mark range calculation requires product/chain differentiation and stationary points; odd symmetry is separately established from the graph/function and belongs to graph properties, not inverses.
The requested substitution and evaluation are a single definite-integration method; trigonometric identities and limits are not separately marked.
The median is obtained from the area under the stated continuous density, with the diagram supplying its shape; integration and descriptive-statistics labels are not independently assessed.
The five marks are for a contradiction proof that an integer root cannot exist; polynomial rearrangement supports the proof but is not a separate retained skill.
Chord length uses triangle trigonometry and the shaded area uses the reflex sector formula with the given radian angle. Coordinate geometry is not independently marked.
The question compares two explicit growth models and proves their ordering, making model/graph interpretation primary; the final six-mark interval calculation independently differentiates the models.
Bearing, speeds, angles, line intersection, arrival times, and minimum separation are all computed from three-dimensional position vectors; triangle geometry is not independently assessed.
The logistic differential equation is differentiated, its maximum growth rate is optimized, and its solution is obtained by separation/partial fractions and integration.

The derivative is integrated and the initial value determines the constant. Differentiation is supplied as the given derivative rather than a separate student-assessed operation, but the controlled Calculus classification remains appropriate.
The question determines when a finite limit exists and evaluates it by repeated l’Hôpital differentiation; the assessed objective is the limit calculation rather than generic differentiation.
Normal tail probabilities determine each competitor's throw probability, then five-trial binomial probabilities determine qualification; descriptive statistics are not assessed.
Implicit derivatives, inflection points, and tangent lines account for the dominant assessed method. Curve sketches and rational-point line intersections are independently marked supporting work.
The full investigation is about Vieta relations, real versus complex roots, and factoring cubic/quartic polynomials.

Derivative and stationary-point work are central. The roots/inequality, absolute-value graph transformation, and trigonometric equation-solving each receive independent marked work and are retained selectively.
Code counting and factor-theorem/polynomial determination are the main marked work; the final cubic sketch has direct graph-feature marks. No probability-model method is assessed.
Arguments of complex products and the ten-mark induction proof are the explicit assessed methods; no separate triangle-geometry method is required.
Midpoint/distance coordinates determine the circle and cone dimensions. No vector-line method is independently assessed.

The second part explicitly applies the right-triangle area formula to the three side expressions. The preceding identity is algebraic setup and does not warrant retaining the production binomial label as a separate primary classification.
The given derivative must be integrated and the point condition determines the constant; differentiation itself is supplied data, not the assessed operation.
The product and sum of roots determine the real parameter in a quartic equation; Vieta/root relations are polynomial-theorem work, not differentiation.
The question applies independence and the lower/upper bounds for an intersection probability; these are probability-model constraints, with no sequence method present.
Implicit product-rule differentiation is followed by the stationary-point condition to prove that no local extrema occur.

Every part asks for the largest interval on which a shifted cosine has an inverse, determined by one-to-one behavior; graphing is evidence for the inverse-domain decision rather than a separate retained skill.
The homogeneous differential equation is solved by substitution and integration, then zero gradient is interpreted as an application of the derivative.
Regression coefficients, correlation, and prediction from a data table are descriptive-statistics calculations; the prior algebraic labels are unsupported by the question.
Parts (a) and (d) use normal standardization/quantiles, (c)(i) is explicitly conditional, and (b)/(c)(ii) use binomial discrete probabilities.
The derivative and tangent condition, the solid-of-revolution integral, and the chain-rule composition derivative are all explicitly marked Calculus methods.

The marks cover vector equations, skew-line testing, plane equations, and closest-point geometry. The equation-solving step is embedded in the vector method and does not need a separate inequality label.
The supplied graph and the requested maximum/intercept coordinates directly assess graph features; the final enclosed-area calculation independently uses a definite integral.
The task finds the common ratio and the least index satisfying a geometric-series sum inequality; logarithmic manipulation is only a way to solve the sequence condition.
The 11% decrease determines k through an exponential equation/logarithm, and the same exponential model is then evaluated at 2041.
The coefficient condition is solved by selecting the relevant term of a binomial expansion and equating coefficients; no statistical-inference method is present.

The normalization condition and median are both properties of the stated continuous probability density. Integration is the calculation mechanism rather than an additional student-facing classification.

The angle is computed from a scalar product/Argand vector representation; the limiting angle is a distinct limit calculation. Complex numbers are only a representational alternative, not an assessed complex-number topic.
The volume model is given; the required operation is a related-rate chain-rule calculation after solving for the relevant height.
The cosine rule determines the diagonal and the area is built from two triangle areas; the trigonometric equation is supporting work within the triangle-geometry method.
Power-sum construction and induction dominate the question; the later derivative identity and repeated l'Hopital limit are independently marked Calculus work.
Cone/sphere/ellipsoid surface-area derivations use integration and differentiation; the explicit f(kx) stretch is a genuine secondary geometric-transformation method.
First- and second-derivative optimization establishes the minimum and pole decision; secant/cosecant identities and right-triangle ratios are independently used in the derivative evaluation.
The angle condition, line directions, shortest distance, plane normal, and cone positions are all vector/line/plane geometry; the intermediate quadratic does not merit a separate algebra tag.
